meta.section: Psychological, Social, and Biological Foundations of Behavior
meta.method: Clean-room: written in the main session from the public content-outline topic list and the cited open sources only. No MCAT question from any provider (AAMC, Khan Academy, UWorld, Kaplan, Blueprint, Jack Westin, Princeton Review) was read while writing. All studies, names and numbers are invented.

P1.title: Napping, stress and memory for word pairs
P1.text:
Sleep is thought to help stabilize newly learned information, a process called consolidation. Researchers tested whether a short afternoon nap improves retention of verbal material, and whether acute stress during the same period affects retention.

Ninety university students aged 18 to 24, all reporting 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night, took part. At 1:00 pm, each participant studied 40 pairs of unrelated nouns (for example, lantern and river) shown one pair at a time on a screen. Participants were then shown the first word of each pair and asked to type the second, and they kept studying until they could correctly produce at least 60% of the pairs.

Participants were then randomly assigned to one of three 60-minute conditions. In the nap condition, participants lay in a darkened room while electrodes recorded their brain activity (EEG), and they were allowed to sleep. In the rest condition, participants stayed awake in a lit room and watched a documentary about coastal wildlife. In the stress condition, participants stayed awake and spent part of the hour preparing and giving a short speech to two evaluators who offered no encouraging feedback, followed by mental arithmetic under time pressure. Saliva samples for cortisol were taken just before the 60-minute period and 20 minutes after it ended.

At 5:00 pm, all participants were again shown the first word of each pair and asked to type the second. Results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1

| Condition | n | Pairs recalled at 5:00 pm (mean %) | Change in salivary cortisol (nmol/L) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nap | 30 | 78 | -1.2 |
| Rest | 30 | 66 | -0.8 |
| Stress | 30 | 61 | +6.5 |

Within the nap condition, 18 participants reached slow-wave sleep according to their EEG records. These participants recalled a mean of 84% of the pairs, compared with 69% for the 12 nap participants who did not reach that stage. The researchers concluded that slow-wave sleep strengthens newly learned associations and that acute stress after learning interferes with their retention.

P2.title: Neighborhood income, health and daily life
P2.text:
Public health researchers have long observed that health outcomes differ between neighborhoods within the same city. A research team surveyed 2,400 adults living in 40 neighborhoods of a mid-sized city to examine how neighborhood income relates to health and to features of daily life.

Neighborhoods were grouped into four quartiles by median household income, from Quartile 1 (lowest) to Quartile 4 (highest), with ten neighborhoods and about 600 respondents in each quartile. Respondents rated their own health as excellent, very good, good, fair, or poor. They also reported how many neighbors they could ask for help in an emergency, such as needing a ride to a clinic. The team used city records to measure the distance from each respondent's home to the nearest full-service grocery store. Selected results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1

| Income quartile | Rated own health fair or poor (%) | Neighbors who could be asked for help (mean) | Distance to full-service grocery store (median, km) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (lowest) | 31 | 2.1 | 3.4 |
| 2 | 24 | 2.6 | 2.2 |
| 3 | 17 | 2.9 | 1.5 |
| 4 (highest) | 11 | 2.8 | 1.1 |

Within every quartile, respondents who named three or more neighbors they could ask for help were 5 to 7 percentage points less likely to rate their health as fair or poor than respondents who named two or fewer. In Quartile 1, 62% of respondents rented their homes, compared with 18% in Quartile 4. The team concluded that living in a low-income neighborhood harms residents' health, partly by limiting access to resources and partly by weakening the networks residents can draw on.

questions.text: Which EEG pattern would most likely have been recorded from the 18 nap participants during the stage of sleep that the researchers linked to better recall?
options: Low-amplitude, high-frequency beta waves
Sleep spindles and K-complexes as the main features
High-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves
Alpha waves of moderate frequency and amplitude
questions.solution: Slow-wave sleep is NREM stage 3, marked by high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves. Beta waves dominate alert wakefulness and alpha waves appear in relaxed wakefulness and early stage 1. Sleep spindles and K-complexes are the hallmarks of stage 2, the stage before slow-wave sleep.

questions.text: The comparison between nap participants who did and did not reach slow-wave sleep does not, on its own, show that slow-wave sleep caused better recall. Which change to the study would best address this limitation?
options: Recruiting enough additional nap participants that the subgroups who did and did not reach slow-wave sleep are equal in size
Measuring salivary cortisol every 10 minutes throughout the nap rather than only before and after the 60-minute period
Testing recall again at 9:00 pm to see whether the advantage of reaching slow-wave sleep persists over a longer delay
Randomly assigning nap participants to undisturbed naps or to naps in which slow-wave sleep is interrupted by quiet tones
questions.solution: Participants were not assigned to reach slow-wave sleep or not; they sorted themselves, so the two subgroups may differ in other ways (for example, how tired they were). Randomly assigning some naps to have slow-wave sleep selectively interrupted makes slow-wave sleep the manipulated variable, which is what a causal claim needs. Equal subgroup sizes, more cortisol samples and a later test leave the self-selection problem in place.

provenance.kind: research-design reasoning on the invented study

questions.text: Which conclusion about the rest and stress conditions is best supported by the information in the passage?
options: The stress condition was accompanied by a rise in cortisol and by lower recall than the rest condition.
The stress task impaired encoding of the word pairs, so fewer pairs were stored in memory.
The rise in cortisol was the direct cause of the lower recall in the stress condition.
Watching the documentary lowered cortisol enough to protect the word pairs from being forgotten.
questions.solution: The table shows cortisol rising by 6.5 nmol/L and recall of 61% in the stress condition, against a small fall in cortisol and 66% recall in the rest condition; option A only describes this. Encoding was finished before the conditions began, since everyone studied to the same 60% criterion first, so B is wrong. Stress was manipulated but cortisol was only measured, and the stress task also involved distraction and effort, so cortisol cannot be singled out as the cause (C). The rest condition's cortisol change is tiny and nothing shows it protected memory (D).

provenance.kind: data reading on the invented study

questions.text: The change in cortisol in the stress condition most likely resulted from which sequence of events?
options: The hypothalamus released corticotropin-releasing hormone, the anterior pituitary released ACTH, and the adrenal cortex released cortisol.
Sympathetic nerves stimulated the adrenal medulla, which released cortisol directly into the bloodstream.
The hypothalamus released corticotropin-releasing hormone, the posterior pituitary released ACTH, and the adrenal medulla released cortisol.
Parasympathetic nerves stimulated the adrenal cortex, which released cortisol directly into the bloodstream.
questions.solution: Cortisol comes from the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis: corticotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus causes the anterior pituitary to release ACTH, which makes the adrenal cortex secrete cortisol. Sympathetic nerves act on the adrenal medulla, which releases epinephrine and norepinephrine, not cortisol. The posterior pituitary makes no ACTH, and the parasympathetic system does not drive the stress response.

questions.text: Suppose a fourth group of participants had studied a second list of 40 noun pairs during the 60-minute period. If their recall of the first list at 5:00 pm were lower than that of the rest condition, this result would best illustrate:
options: proactive interference.
retroactive interference.
the serial position effect.
encoding specificity.
questions.solution: New learning (the second list) disrupting memory for earlier learning (the first list) is retroactive interference. Proactive interference runs the other way: old learning disrupts new learning. The serial position effect concerns better recall of items at the start and end of a list, and encoding specificity concerns the match between study and test conditions.

questions.text: A critic argues that the rest condition recalled less than the nap condition because the documentary itself disrupted memory for the word pairs, not because rest participants stayed awake. Which finding, if true, would most weaken the critic's argument?
options: Rest participants could describe many specific details from the documentary when asked about it at 5:00 pm.
Nap participants slept for an average of 47 minutes of their 60-minute period, according to their EEG records.
Recall in the stress condition, in which participants also stayed awake, was lower than recall in the rest condition.
Awake participants who rested with eyes closed and no documentary recalled about as many pairs as the rest condition.
questions.solution: If staying awake without any documentary gives the same recall as staying awake with it, the documentary is not what lowered recall, so the critic's argument loses its basis. Option A, if anything, supports the critic: the documentary was encoded and could have interfered. Sleep duration (B) and the stress result (C) say nothing about whether the documentary itself mattered.

questions.text: The longer distances to full-service grocery stores in lower-income neighborhoods are best described as an example of:
options: spatial inequality.
residential segregation.
relative poverty.
social reproduction.
questions.solution: Spatial inequality is the unequal distribution of resources and services across places, such as grocery stores being farther from poorer neighborhoods. Residential segregation is the separation of social groups into different neighborhoods, which may contribute to the pattern but is not the pattern itself. Relative poverty describes having much less than others in one's society, and social reproduction describes inequality being passed from one generation to the next.

provenance.kind: standard sociology term; not defined in OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e

questions.text: Which statement about the relationship between neighborhood income and the number of neighbors respondents could ask for help is best supported by Table 1?
options: The number rises with every step up in neighborhood income, from Quartile 1 to Quartile 4.
The number shows no relationship with neighborhood income across the four quartiles.
The number rises from Quartile 1 to Quartile 3 and changes little between Quartiles 3 and 4.
Differences in this number account for the whole difference in health between Quartiles 1 and 4.
questions.solution: The means are 2.1, 2.6, 2.9 and 2.8: a clear rise to Quartile 3, then a slight dip, so it does not rise at every step (A) and is not unrelated (B). The within-quartile gap linked to social ties is 5 to 7 percentage points, far smaller than the 20-point health gap between Quartiles 1 and 4, so ties cannot account for all of it (D).

provenance.kind: data reading on the invented study

questions.text: Which is the strongest objection to the team's conclusion that living in a low-income neighborhood harms residents' health?
options: A total of 2,400 adults spread over 40 neighborhoods is too small a sample to compare four income groups.
People whose health is already poor may move into, or be unable to leave, lower-cost neighborhoods.
Ratings of one's own health have no relationship to measures of health made by doctors or to later illness.
The survey asked only about neighbors in an emergency, so everyday social ties were not measured at all.
questions.solution: A one-time survey shows an association but not its direction. If poor health leads people into, or keeps them in, cheaper neighborhoods, the neighborhood need not be harming anyone. About 600 respondents per quartile is ample for this comparison (A). Self-rated health is a widely used measure that tracks later illness, so C is false. D questions one detail of the networks explanation but not the central claim that the neighborhood harms health.

provenance.kind: research-design reasoning on the invented study

questions.text: A sociologist argues that grocery chains, landlords and city officials with more economic and political power decide where stores and services are located, in ways that benefit wealthier residents. This explanation is most consistent with:
options: functionalism.
symbolic interactionism.
social exchange theory.
conflict theory.
questions.solution: Conflict theory explains social patterns as the result of groups competing for scarce resources, with more powerful groups shaping outcomes to their own advantage. Functionalism asks how a pattern helps society run, symbolic interactionism focuses on the meanings people create in everyday interaction, and social exchange theory explains behavior through individuals weighing costs and rewards.

questions.text: The finding that respondents who could ask more neighbors for help reported better health within every quartile is most consistent with the idea that health is related to:
options: cultural capital.
human capital.
social capital.
economic capital.
questions.solution: Social capital is the set of resources, such as help and information, that people can draw on through their social networks. Cultural capital is knowledge, tastes and skills valued by a society, human capital is a person's own education and skills, and economic capital is money and property. Because the comparison is made within each income quartile, neighborhood income is held roughly constant, which points away from economic capital.

provenance.kind: standard sociology term; not defined in OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e

questions.text: Suppose that over the next ten years, many long-term renters in Quartile 1 neighborhoods are replaced by higher-income newcomers. The share of Quartile 1 residents rating their health as fair or poor then falls, although the long-term residents who stayed report no change in their health. Which explanation best fits these results?
options: Rising rents increased the incomes of the long-term residents who stayed, which improved their health.
The fall reflects a change in who lives in these neighborhoods, not better health among those already there.
The newcomers report their own health less accurately than long-term residents do.
The newcomers brought more grocery stores, which improved the health of everyone in these neighborhoods.
questions.solution: When healthier, higher-income people replace residents with poorer health, the neighborhood's average improves even though no individual's health changed: a change in the population's composition. A and D contradict the statement that the long-term residents' health did not change, and nothing supports C.

questions.text: A participant can just detect that a 200 g weight has become heavier when 4 g are added to it. According to Weber's law, about how much weight must be added to a 500 g weight for the same participant to just detect the change?
options: 4 g
questions.solution: Weber's law states that the just noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the original stimulus. Here the fraction is 4/200 = 0.02, so for 500 g the change needed is 0.02 x 500 = 10 g. 4 g wrongly treats the difference as a fixed amount.

questions.text: A fitness app awards a badge after an unpredictable number of logged workouts, averaging one badge for every five workouts. Compared with awarding a badge after every workout, this schedule would most likely produce:
options: a high, steady rate of logging that continues longer once badges stop.
a pause in logging after each badge, followed by a burst of activity.
logging that speeds up as the expected time of the next badge approaches.
logging that stops more quickly once badges are no longer given.
questions.solution: A badge after an unpredictable number of responses is a variable-ratio schedule, which produces a high, steady response rate with little pause and the greatest resistance to extinction. A pause after each reward is typical of fixed-ratio schedules, and speeding up as a reward time approaches is the fixed-interval pattern. Behavior reinforced every time (continuous reinforcement) extinguishes faster, not slower.

questions.text: A clinic nurse decides that a patient who has arrived late for a third appointment does not care about his health, without considering that he depends on an unreliable bus route. The next week, when the nurse arrives late for her own shift, she blames heavy traffic. The contrast between her two explanations best illustrates:
options: the fundamental attribution error.
the self-serving bias.
the actor-observer bias.
the just-world hypothesis.
questions.solution: The actor-observer bias is the tendency to explain other people's behavior by their dispositions while explaining one's own behavior by the situation, which is exactly the contrast here. The fundamental attribution error covers only the first half (judging the patient). The self-serving bias concerns explaining one's own successes and failures and says nothing about judging others. The just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve.

questions.text: According to one version of the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia, excess dopamine activity in limbic regions of the brain is most closely associated with which symptoms?
options: Reduced speech and little emotion shown in the face
Social withdrawal and a lack of motivation
Impaired working memory and difficulty sustaining attention
Hallucinations and delusions
questions.solution: In this version of the hypothesis, too much dopamine activity in the limbic system is linked to positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, while too little dopamine in the prefrontal cortex is linked to negative symptoms such as reduced speech, blunted emotional expression, withdrawal and low motivation. Working-memory and attention problems are cognitive symptoms, also tied to prefrontal function rather than limbic dopamine excess.

questions.text: A 14-year-old notices that her teachers seem surprised whenever she answers a science question correctly. Over the school year she comes to see herself as 'not a science person.' This change in her self-concept best illustrates:
options: the looking-glass self.
the Pygmalion effect.
identity foreclosure.
social facilitation.
questions.solution: Cooley's looking-glass self holds that people build their self-concept partly from how they believe others see them, which is what happens here. The Pygmalion effect is about others' expectations changing a person's performance, not self-concept. Identity foreclosure is committing to an identity without exploring alternatives, and social facilitation is performing simple tasks better in the presence of others.

questions.text: Before a meeting, most members of a hospital committee slightly favor delaying a new procedure until more data are available. After discussing it together, the committee votes to postpone the procedure indefinitely, a more cautious position than the members held on average beforehand. This shift best illustrates:
options: groupthink.
group polarization.
social loafing.
deindividuation.
questions.solution: Group polarization is the strengthening of a group's initial leaning after discussion: a mild preference for caution became a stronger one. Groupthink is members setting aside their own views to fit what they believe the group consensus is, which the scenario does not describe. Social loafing is reduced effort on pooled tasks, and deindividuation is a loss of self-awareness in groups.

questions.text: Over 30 years, a country's death rate has fallen sharply because of improved sanitation and vaccination, while its birth rate has stayed high. According to demographic transition theory, the country's population is most likely:
options: stable, because birth and death rates are both high.
stable or shrinking, because birth and death rates are both low.
growing rapidly, because births far exceed deaths.
growing more slowly, because the birth rate is falling.
questions.solution: A falling death rate with a still-high birth rate is the second stage of the demographic transition, when births far outnumber deaths and the population grows rapidly. High birth and death rates describe the first stage, falling birth rates the third, and low rates of both the fourth.

questions.text: A first-year resident physician who is also the parent of a newborn finds that the hospital's overnight shifts and her child's needs make demands she cannot meet at the same time. This situation is best described as:
options: role strain.
role exit.
status inconsistency.
role conflict.
questions.solution: Role conflict arises when the demands of two or more roles are incompatible, here physician and parent. Role strain is too much demand within a single role, role exit is leaving a role, and status inconsistency is holding statuses ranked differently (for example, high education with low income).
